title: Latin America
hook: base communities reading the Bible together, and a Pentecostal wave
carry: the bible read by the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, China's churches, one with its name on the gate and one with the curtains drawn. Your line was the seed underground. What did you plant that you're still waiting on? Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

A village chapel with a tin roof. The Gospel has just been read: Jesus feeding a hungry crowd. And then, instead of a sermon, a question goes around the benches. What do you hear? A fisherman says the crowd was hungry because somebody kept the bread. A grandmother says the disciples wanted to send people away, and Jesus said no, you feed them. A teenager asks why their own village is still hungry. Nobody in the room has studied theology. Everybody in the room knows hunger. Today, Latin America, where the Bible got passed around the benches.
screen: `A TIN ROOF, A GOSPEL, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: They were called base communities: small groups of poor Catholics, often led by lay people rather than priests, meeting to read the Bible against their own lives. In Nicaragua, a priest named Ernesto Cardenal wrote down the conversations of the farmers and fishermen in his island parish, and the book became The Gospel in Solentiname. Here is a passage from Luke that sounds different in rooms like those. Jesus stands up in the synagogue in his hometown, is handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, and reads, in the King James Bible: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." To the poor. Read in a tin-roofed chapel, that line doesn't sound like a metaphor. Alongside these groups and their pastors grew what was called liberation theology, which spoke of God's special care for the poor. It stirred real argument. Supporters said it was simply the Gospel read honestly from the bottom. Some Catholic leaders, Rome among them, warned against borrowing ideas from Marxism, and the debate was carried on inside the church. Meanwhile a second wave was rising in the same neighborhoods: Pentecostal churches, small congregations in rented rooms with guitars and healing prayer and preachers from the block. Their style looked nothing like the base communities, and the two did not always get along. But both put the Bible in ordinary hands and asked what it said to people who had very little. In Matthew, Jesus says it in a prayer: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes."
screen: `BASE COMMUNITIES: THE BIBLE ON THE BENCHES.`
`A PENTECOSTAL WAVE ON THE SAME BLOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read like the benches did. Settle, and breathe. Take the line from Luke: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor. Say it slowly in your head, twice. Then ask the base community's question: what do I hear? Not what a scholar would say. What it says about your street, your week, the people you passed today. Let one honest answer come. Then pick someone, a friend, a partner, a parent, and decide when you could read a short passage together and ask each other the same question. If you pray, you can pray the line back. The bell holds the time.
Latin America. Base communities reading scripture together in small, poor parishes, and a Pentecostal wave in the same streets: the Bible in ordinary hands.
Your line: the bible read by the poor. Today, read a passage with a friend, even by text message, and each say one thing you hear in it. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Small Bible-sharing groups meet in homes and parishes across Latin America, reading a passage aloud and talking about what it says to their own lives, while Pentecostal congregations gather for lively worship, preaching and prayer for healing.

notes: The hook scene is an illustrative composite in the style of the Solentiname dialogues, not a quotation; the feeding story is not cited because no lines are quoted. Confirm it is fair to present it this way.
Claims rule: base communities described as 'small groups of poor Catholics, often led by lay people'; no counts or dates. Confirm.
Solentiname: Cardenal's parish on an island in Lake Nicaragua; the book records campesinos discussing the Sunday Gospel. Confirm 'farmers and fishermen in his island parish'.

Liberation theology debate: 'Some Catholic leaders, Rome among them, warned against mixing the Gospel with political theory' summarizes the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's instructions (1984, 1986) without dates. Confirm fair to both sides; 'God's special care for the poor' glosses 'preferential option for the poor' (not named).
'the two did not always get along' (base communities and Pentecostals): general, unranked; confirm.
Pentecostalism kept brief because day 975 covers it.
